findings.text: For 2026, publishers planned to put more effort into YouTube (+74 percentage points net), AI platforms (+61), and TikTok (+56), and less effort into X (−52), Facebook (−23), and old-style Google Search (−25).

findings.text: Publishers were experimenting with Substack as a distribution channel and expanding vertical video, including a curated vertical-video feed in the New York Times app’s watch tab.

findings.text: Publishers were more concerned about creators taking audience time and attention (70% somewhat or very concerned) than about losing talent to creators (39%).
findings.evidence: The report gives 70% as somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

findings.text: Planned responses to the creator wave included making journalists more like creators (76%), partnering with creators for distribution (50%), hiring creators (31%), and creating a joint venture such as a creator studio (28%).
findings.evidence: The report’s Q20 chart lists the four planned initiatives and their percentages: 76%, 50%, 31%, and 28%, respectively.

findings.text: The report notes that building journalists’ independent profiles may help them leave with their audiences, citing Dave Jorgenson’s departure from the Washington Post and the subsequent collapse in reach of its Universe YouTube channel.
findings.evidence: The report says journalists may gain confidence to leave with their followers and describes the Post’s Universe channel reach crumbling after Jorgenson set up his own enterprise.

findings.text: Between November 2024 and November 2025, organic Google search traffic to more than 2,500 sites declined by 33% globally and 38% in the United States; the report says lifestyle and utility publishers may have been more affected than hard-news publishers.

findings.text: The report says helping journalists build independent profiles may give them confidence to leave with their followers; it describes Dave Jorgenson’s departure from the Washington Post and says reach of the Post’s “Universe” YouTube channel crumbled almost overnight.
findings.evidence: Another significant risk is that, by helping journalists to build their independent profile, they may be giving them confidence to leave – taking their followers with them. The Washington Post’s TikTok guy, Dave Jorgenson, worked at the company for eight years picking up many prizes in the process before setting up on his own. Almost overnight the reach of the Post’s ‘Universe’ YouTube channel, which hosted his videos, crumbled, overtaken by Jorgenson’s new enterprise LNI (Local News International), according to data from Rival IQ.
